Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

DAVOS, Switzerland (CNN) -- The worldwide economic recession has exposed a "crisis of global governance" that can only be addressed by the radical reform of the United Nations, former U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said Wednesday as the World Economic Forum got under way in Switzerland. Kofi Annan says the United Nations needs to be reformed. "The current architecture of managing global affairs is broken and needs to be fixed," Annan said on the opening morning of the five-day annual meeting of global political and business leaders. "We have major new players coming on the scene and they need to be integrated and given a voice." Referring to the U.N. Security Council, which gives permanent places and vetoing powers to the U.S., the UK, Russia, China and France, Annan said: "We cannot continue to run the world based on countries that won a war 60 years ago. It's either destructive competition or cooperation. We live in an interdependent world and the only way to move forward is to cooperate." Annan is one of six co-chairs at this year's WEF gathering, along with news tycoon Rupert Murdoch, HSBC Chairman Stephen Green, Werner Wenning of the German chemical group Bayer, Indian industrialist Anand G. Mahindra and Maria Ramos, Chief Executive of the South African transport group Transnet. He also urged delegates to address three interconnected challenges: the global recession, energy and security, and climate change. "It is important leaders work on ways of finding effective, far-reaching policies -- even if they are radical -- that will allow us to create sustainable economic growth and create jobs for those who are out of jobs," Annan said. Newscorp. CEO Murdoch said delegates needed to be "absolutely honest about where the world is at this point," warning that the consequences of $50 trillion being wiped off personal fortunes had left people feeling "depressed and traumatized." "We've been living in the Western world way above our means. We've been on a great binge and it's come to an end and we have to live though the correction," Murdoch said. But he said the downturn offered a chance to set about tackling issues of energy sufficiency and pollution. "We must treat this crisis, whether it lasts for a year or five years, as an opportunity to set goals for how we want to come out of it. This is a time to shape the policies to help to solve some of those problems." HSBC boss Green said the banking industry needed to admit that it had not "covered itself in glory" in contributing to the collapse of the financial industry and called for continuing government intervention to "stop a nasty recession spiraling down into something else." But he said the major banks could contribute to solving the crisis as well: "I do not believe for a moment that you can have a successful economy without successful and properly functioning international capital markets." Wenning said he didn't expect any solutions to emerge from this year's meeting, but hoped delegates could achieve "a joint understanding of the reasons for the financial crisis" and called for a return to "the basics of sustainable behavior." "If we are really able to address these mega-challenges of the future then we would be able to restore the trust in leadership -- and I believe the world needs leadership." Political leaders will join the discussions later Wednesday with Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin both due to deliver agenda-setting addresses.

Security Council, which grants permanent seats and veto powers to the United States, the United Kingdom, Russia, China and France, Annan said: “We cannot continue to run the world based on countries that won a war 60 years ago. It’s either destructive competition or cooperation. We live in an interdependent world, and the only way to move forward is to cooperate.”

Annan is one of six co-chairs of this year’s WEF gathering, alongside media tycoon Rupert Murdoch, HSBC Chairman Stephen Green, Werner Wenning of the German chemical group Bayer, Indian industrialist Anand G. Mahindra and Maria Ramos, chief executive of the South African transport group Transnet.

He also urged delegates to address three interconnected challenges: the global recession, energy and security, and climate change.

“It is important leaders work on ways of finding effective, far-reaching policies—even if they are radical—that will allow us to create sustainable economic growth and create jobs for those who are out of jobs,” Annan said.

News Corp. CEO Murdoch said delegates needed to be “absolutely honest about where the world is at this point,” warning that the loss of $50 trillion in personal fortunes had left people feeling “depressed and traumatized.”

“We’ve been living in the Western world way above our means. We’ve been on a great binge, and it’s come to an end, and we have to live through the correction,” Murdoch said.

However, he said the downturn offered an opportunity to begin tackling the issues of energy sufficiency and pollution.

“We must treat this crisis, whether it lasts for a year or five years, as an opportunity to set goals for how we want to come out of it. This is a time to shape the policies to help to solve some of those problems.”

DAVOS, Switzerland (CNN) — Former U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan called for sweeping changes to the United Nations on Wednesday, arguing that the global recession had revealed a broader failure in the way international affairs are governed.

Speaking at the start of the World Economic Forum’s five-day annual gathering of political and business leaders in Switzerland, Annan said existing systems for managing global issues were no longer effective. Emerging powers, he added, must be brought into those structures and given meaningful representation.

Turning to the U.N. Security Council, Annan criticized an arrangement that grants permanent membership and veto authority to the United States, Britain, Russia, China and France. He said the world could not continue to be governed according to which nations had won a war six decades earlier. Countries now faced a choice between damaging rivalry and cooperation, he said, emphasizing that progress in an interdependent world depended on working together.

Annan is serving as one of six co-chairs of this year’s forum. The others are News Corp. chief Rupert Murdoch; HSBC Chairman Stephen Green; Werner Wenning of German chemicals company Bayer; Indian industrialist Anand G. Mahindra; and Maria Ramos, chief executive of South African transportation group Transnet.

He also asked participants to confront three linked problems: the worldwide downturn, energy and security, and climate change. Annan said leaders needed to develop effective, ambitious policies—even radical ones—that could generate sustainable growth and provide employment for people who had lost their jobs.

Murdoch said those attending the forum must be completely candid about the state of the world. With $50 trillion erased from personal wealth, he warned, many people had been left traumatized and deeply discouraged.

According to Murdoch, the West had spent far beyond its resources, enjoying an extended period of excess that had now ended. Society would have to endure the resulting correction, he said. At the same time, he argued that the slump created an opening to address adequate energy supplies and pollution.

Whether the crisis continued for one year or five, Murdoch said, it should be used to decide what the world should look like when the downturn was over. The moment offered an opportunity to design policies capable of resolving some of those long-term difficulties.

Green acknowledged that banks had not distinguished themselves through their role in the financial sector’s collapse. He urged governments to remain involved so that a severe recession did not deteriorate into something worse.

Nevertheless, Green maintained that major banks also had a part to play in resolving the emergency. A strong economy, he said, was impossible without healthy, properly operating international capital markets.

Wenning said he did not anticipate that the meeting would produce concrete answers. He did, however, hope participants could reach a shared view of what had caused the financial crisis and renew their commitment to the fundamentals of sustainable conduct.

Successfully dealing with the major challenges ahead, Wenning said, could rebuild confidence in leadership—something he believed the world urgently required.

Political figures were scheduled to enter the debate later Wednesday. Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin were both expected to give major speeches intended to help define the forum’s agenda.

### Kofi Annan Calls for Global Governance Reform

Speaking at the World Economic Forum, former United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan argued that the global recession had revealed not only serious economic weaknesses but also a deeper crisis in international governance. The institutions created to manage global affairs, he said, no longer adequately reflected the distribution of power and influence in the modern world.

Annan called for radical reform of the United Nations and other multilateral institutions. Emerging economies and developing countries needed a stronger voice in international decision-making, particularly as their economic and political importance continued to grow. Institutions that remained dominated by an outdated balance of power would struggle to command legitimacy or organize an effective response to global problems.

The recession also demonstrated how closely national economies had become connected. Financial instability in one part of the world could quickly affect businesses, workers, and governments elsewhere. No country, however powerful, could restore stability by acting alone. Governments therefore needed to coordinate economic policies, rebuild confidence, stimulate growth, and ensure that recovery measures produced employment rather than merely protecting financial institutions.

Annan linked the economic crisis to other urgent challenges, including energy security and climate change. These issues could not be treated separately because decisions in one area inevitably affected the others. Efforts to revive economic growth, for example, would influence energy demand and greenhouse-gas emissions, while dependence on scarce or unstable energy supplies could create further economic and political risks.

He also warned that patterns of excessive consumption in Western countries were environmentally and economically unsustainable. A return to the same habits that had contributed to financial instability and placed increasing pressure on natural resources would not provide a durable recovery. Instead, governments and businesses needed to pursue forms of growth that were more balanced, inclusive, and environmentally responsible.

Addressing these interconnected threats would require bold policies and sustained international cooperation. Reforming global institutions, expanding representation, creating jobs, improving energy security, and confronting climate change were not separate ambitions but parts of a common agenda. Annan’s central message was that the crisis offered an opportunity to build a fairer and more effective international system—provided world leaders were willing to move beyond outdated structures and narrow national interests.

# Annan calls for sweeping U.N. reform amid global economic crisis

**DAVOS, Switzerland (CNN)** — Former United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan called for radical reform of the U.N. and other international institutions at the World Economic Forum in Davos, arguing that the global recession had exposed the weaknesses of a system designed for a different era.

Speaking as political and business leaders gathered in the Swiss Alps to confront the deepening economic downturn, Annan said the crisis demonstrated how closely connected the world had become — and how poorly existing institutions were equipped to respond.

He urged governments to give emerging economies and developing nations a stronger voice in global decision-making, warning that institutions would lose legitimacy if they failed to reflect shifting economic and political power.

The former U.N. chief also stressed that the recession’s effects would extend far beyond financial markets. Falling investment, declining trade and reduced aid threatened to push millions of people deeper into poverty, particularly in countries that had played little role in creating the crisis.

Annan argued that reform should include a more representative U.N. system, closer coordination among international organizations and stronger mechanisms for addressing threats that cross national borders, including financial instability, climate change and food insecurity.

His appeal came as the Davos meeting was dominated by debate over how to restore confidence in the global economy. Leaders faced pressure to overhaul financial regulation while avoiding protectionist policies that could further weaken trade and growth.

Annan warned that national responses alone would be insufficient. In an interconnected world, he said, governments must treat cooperation not as an ideal but as a practical necessity.

The challenge, he suggested, was not simply to revive the old economic order, but to build a fairer and more accountable international system from the crisis.

**Davos opens under twin clouds of recession and climate risk**

**DAVOS, Switzerland, Jan. 28, 2009** — The World Economic Forum opened with business and political leaders acknowledging that the global financial crisis had exposed serious weaknesses in corporate conduct, financial regulation and international governance.

Former UN Secretary-General **Kofi Annan** said the turmoil demonstrated how closely connected the world had become—and how poorly existing institutions were equipped to manage global problems. He called for more effective and inclusive governance, warning that poorer countries, despite having contributed least to both the financial crisis and climate change, were likely to suffer the gravest consequences.

News Corp. Chairman **Rupert Murdoch** offered a bleak assessment of the economy, saying the downturn was worsening and could be the most severe since the Great Depression. He cautioned against expecting a quick recovery and argued that governments needed decisive action to restore confidence and repair banking systems.

**Stephen Green**, chairman of HSBC, said banks had to accept responsibility for the collapse in public trust. The industry could not simply return to business as usual, he said, stressing the need for stronger oversight, greater transparency and a renewed understanding that finance must serve the wider economy. Because markets operate across borders, regulatory reform also had to be internationally coordinated.

Despite the focus on recession, Bayer Chief Executive **Werner Wenning** warned against pushing climate change down the agenda. The financial emergency did not make the environmental threat less urgent, he said. Governments should maintain clear, long-term climate policies, while companies should continue investing in energy efficiency and low-carbon technologies.

The opening-day discussions reflected Davos’s central message: the economic crash was not only a banking failure but also a crisis of governance and confidence. Participants broadly agreed that recovery measures should be linked to institutional reform and should not come at the expense of action on climate change.

# Annan: Economic Downturn Exposes ‘Crisis of Global Governance’

**GENEVA —** Former United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan said the global economic downturn has exposed a deeper “crisis of global governance,” arguing that the world’s leading institutions no longer reflect modern political and economic realities.

Annan said the financial turmoil demonstrated that national governments could not manage interconnected global problems on their own. International institutions, he argued, must become more representative and capable of coordinating responses to crises that cross borders.

He singled out the U.N. Security Council, saying its permanent membership remains rooted in the balance of power that followed World War II. The council’s five veto-wielding permanent members — Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States — have retained their privileged status despite the emergence of new powers and the growing influence of developing regions.

The absence of permanent representation for Africa and Latin America has long fueled demands for reform. Annan said the council’s structure undermines its legitimacy and weakens confidence in international decision-making.

His remarks add urgency to years of stalled negotiations over Security Council expansion. While U.N. members broadly agree that the body should better reflect today’s world, they remain divided over which countries should gain permanent seats and whether any new members should receive veto power.

Annan warned that reform must extend beyond the United Nations to the wider international system. The economic downturn, he said, showed that institutions created for an earlier era were struggling to address modern challenges, including financial instability, poverty, climate change and conflict.

Without broader participation and more effective cooperation, he suggested, global institutions risk losing both public trust and the authority needed to respond to future crises.

**DAVOS, Switzerland, Jan. 28 —** Political and business leaders opened the five-day World Economic Forum on Wednesday under the shadow of a deepening global recession, with the gathering’s six co-chairs calling for coordinated stimulus, stronger financial oversight and resistance to protectionism.

The annual meeting in the Swiss Alpine resort, whose theme is “Shaping the Post-Crisis World,” comes as governments struggle with shrinking output, rising unemployment and a banking crisis that has spread from the United States and Europe to emerging economies.

More than 2,500 participants from nearly 100 countries are expected to attend, including heads of government, central bankers, corporate executives, economists and leaders of international organizations. The agenda is dominated by the most severe economic downturn in decades and by questions over how governments should redesign financial regulation once the immediate crisis eases.

The meeting’s six co-chairs are former U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan; Cisco Systems Chairman and Chief Executive John Chambers; Renault and Nissan Chief Executive Carlos Ghosn; Mahindra & Mahindra Vice Chairman and Managing Director Anand Mahindra; News Corp. Chairman and Chief Executive Rupert Murdoch; and Maria Ramos, chief executive of South African transport group Transnet.

Their opening message emphasized that national rescue programs would be insufficient unless governments coordinated their actions and addressed a collapse in confidence.

Annan urged leaders to ensure that the poorest countries did not become collateral damage in a crisis that began in wealthier economies. He said the downturn should not push longer-term problems—including poverty, food security and climate change—off the international agenda. International institutions, he argued, must be strengthened and made more representative of emerging and developing countries.

Chambers stressed the role of technology and communications infrastructure in improving productivity and creating jobs. He advocated public-private investment in broadband, education and other projects that could produce both immediate employment and longer-term gains, rather than relying only on short-lived measures to stimulate consumption.

Ghosn said the automobile industry’s steep decline illustrated the speed with which the financial shock had spread into the broader economy. He called for measures to restore credit to companies and consumers, while warning that government assistance should not freeze uncompetitive industrial structures in place. Any recovery program, he said, would have to combine emergency support with restructuring and continued investment in cleaner technologies.

Mahindra said emerging markets could help drive a global recovery if they retained access to financing and if governments kept trade open. He warned that protectionist measures, including preferences for domestic companies attached to stimulus packages, could deepen the downturn by inviting retaliation and disrupting international supply chains.

Murdoch focused on restoring confidence among consumers, investors and businesses. He said governments needed to act decisively to stabilize financial institutions but should preserve the incentives for entrepreneurship and private investment that would ultimately be needed to revive growth.

Ramos called for infrastructure spending and development financing, particularly in Africa and other regions where investment in transport, energy and communications could create jobs while removing obstacles to future expansion. She also urged international lenders and donor governments not to retreat from commitments to developing countries as their own budgets came under pressure.

Despite differences in emphasis, the co-chairs broadly supported fiscal action to sustain demand, steps to repair bank balance sheets and tighter—but internationally coordinated—financial regulation. They also warned that economic nationalism could turn a severe recession into a more prolonged global contraction.

The forum is taking place amid widespread criticism of bankers, corporate executives and regulators. Several prominent financial leaders who had been regular Davos participants were absent or keeping a lower profile after huge losses forced governments to provide banks with capital injections, guarantees and emergency loans.

Organizers said the gathering would examine reforms to financial markets, global governance and international institutions, including the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. Energy security, climate change, trade and conflicts in the Middle East and elsewhere also feature on the program, though the recession is expected to dominate discussions.

Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin are due to deliver major speeches at the start of the meeting, giving two of the world’s largest emerging economies an unusually prominent role.

Wen is expected to outline China’s response to slowing growth and falling exports, including Beijing’s multitrillion-yuan stimulus program centered on infrastructure, reconstruction and domestic demand. Delegates will be watching for indications that China is prepared to take further action to sustain growth and contribute to a wider recovery.

Putin, scheduled to give the forum’s opening address, is expected to discuss the causes of the crisis, Russia’s economic response and the need for changes in the global financial system. His appearance comes as Russia faces declining industrial production, pressure on the ruble and sharply lower revenue following the fall in oil and commodity prices.

The two speeches are likely to underscore a shift in the balance of the Davos debate. While the United States and Western Europe remain central to efforts to stabilize the financial system, China, Russia and other emerging powers are demanding a larger voice in writing the rules that will govern the post-crisis economy.

Participants acknowledged that the forum itself cannot enact policy. But they said the meeting could help prepare the ground for decisions at upcoming international gatherings, including talks among the Group of 20 leading economies.

The central question over the five days will be whether governments can coordinate emergency measures without retreating behind national barriers—and whether they can turn a collection of bank rescues and stimulus packages into a credible plan for global recovery.

**CNN Special Report — Davos, Switzerland, January 2009**

**ANCHOR:**  
Global markets are still reeling from the worst financial crisis in decades. Here in Davos, political leaders and corporate executives are warning that the collapse threatens jobs, trade and political stability. But many also see an opportunity to rebuild the institutions governing the global economy. CNN reports from the World Economic Forum.

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Against the snow-covered backdrop of the Swiss Alps, the mood at this year’s World Economic Forum is unusually sober.

Bank failures, frozen credit markets and deepening recession have shaken confidence not only in financial institutions, but in the system of global economic governance itself.

Inside the conference halls, leaders are debating how to prevent the crisis from spreading—and whether it can become a catalyst for reform.

**SOUNDBITE — GOVERNMENT OFFICIAL:**  
“The immediate task is to restore growth and protect employment. But simply returning to the old system is not enough.”

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
One major target is international oversight. The International Monetary Fund and World Bank were created for a different era, when the United States and Europe dominated the global economy. Emerging powers—including China, India and Brazil—are demanding a greater voice.

European leaders are also calling for stronger international rules governing financial markets, warning that capital moves across borders more quickly than regulators can respond.

The banking industry faces its own reckoning. Executives acknowledge that excessive borrowing, complex securities and poorly understood risks helped produce the collapse. Governments have committed enormous sums to stabilize banks, prompting calls for tighter capital requirements, greater transparency and limits on executive compensation.

**SOUNDBITE — BANKING EXECUTIVE:**  
“Trust has been lost. The industry must demonstrate that it can support the real economy rather than simply create risk within the financial system.”

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Yet the debate extends beyond banking.

Some participants argue that massive government stimulus programs could accelerate a transition toward cleaner energy. Investments in renewable power, efficient buildings, public transportation and modern electricity grids, they say, could create jobs while reducing dependence on imported oil.

But with oil prices down sharply and public budgets under pressure, environmental campaigners fear that climate commitments could be postponed.

**SOUNDBITE — ENVIRONMENTAL ADVOCATE:**  
“The financial crisis cannot become an excuse to ignore the climate crisis. Recovery spending will shape energy use for decades.”

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Business leaders see both risk and opportunity. New environmental regulations could raise costs for older industries, but they could also create markets for low-carbon technology, electric vehicles and alternative energy.

The central question in Davos is whether governments can coordinate their response. Protectionism, competitive currency policies and conflicting national regulations could deepen the downturn. Cooperation could produce stronger institutions—and a more balanced global economy.

For years, this gathering celebrated the expansion of global finance. Now its participants are confronting the consequences of that expansion.

The crisis has exposed the system’s weaknesses. Whether it leads to lasting reform—or only temporary repairs—may depend on what leaders do after leaving the mountains.

**CNN, Davos, Switzerland.**
